title: Take One Tablet and Call Me in the Morning
bodyHtml:
Hittite is an extinct language that belongs to the Anatolian branch of the Indo-European language family. It was spoken in the ancient Hittite Empire in second millennium BCE. Hittite was written using a script, called cuneiform, composed of many wedge shapes; an example of cuneiform unrelated to this problem is below.

The excerpt below is a (simplified) phonetic rendering of a cuneiform passage found on a tablet. You do not need to know how the text is pronounced to solve this problem.

našta illuyankan
ḫattešnaz šarā kallišta
kāšawa ezenan iyami
nuwa adanna akuwanna eḫu

našta illuyankaš qadu dumumeššu
šarā úēr nuza eter ekuer
našta palḫan ḫūmandan ekuer
neza ninkēr

ne namma ḫattešnaš kattanta
nūmān pānzi ḫupašiyašša úit
nu illuyankan išḫimanta kalēliēt

imaš úit nukán illuyankan
kuenta dingirmešša kattišši ešer

Its translation into English:

And he called up the snake from the hole: “Behold the feast I’m making! Come to eat and to drink!” And the snake came up with his sons. And they ate and drank. And they drank all the kettles. And they could no longer go down into the hole again. And Hupasiyas came and tied the snake with a rope. The Stormgod came and killed the snake; and the gods were with him.”

assets.alt: Two lines of cuneiform wedge-shaped signs, an example unrelated to the problem

questions.partPrompt: Match the following Hittite word forms with their English translations. Options: (1) snake, (2) hole, (3) came, (4) and, (5) up, (6) drank, (7) ate. Write the number of the matching translation.

Match the following suffixes with their grammatical roles. Options: (1) marker of the infinitive (infinitives are verbs translated with to, such as "to sleep" or "to walk"), (2) plural marker, (3) marker of 3rd person plural past tense verbs, (4) marker of the direct object, (5) marker of the subject, (6) marker for 3rd person singular past tense verbs, (7) marker denoting "and". Write the number of the matching role.

hints.text: The Hittite passage is printed in four stanzas and the English translation follows the same order, sentence by sentence. Before worrying about suffixes, chop both texts into matching chunks: which Hittite words sit in the stretch that becomes "And the snake came up with his sons"?

Several Hittite words show up more than once with slightly different endings. Write those families out side by side, decide what part is the shared stem and what part is the ending, and then look at what the English does differently in each case (who is doing the action, how many of them, whether the word is the doer or the thing acted on). Each ending in F2 can be pinned down by finding two forms of the same stem that differ only in that ending.

Here is the method on a line that is not asked about. The line "kāšawa ezenan iyami" matches "Behold the feast I'm making!" Three Hittite words, three English pieces: kāšawa lines up with "Behold", ezenan with "the feast", and iyami with "I'm making". Notice that the thing being made comes before the verb, so in Hittite the verb tends to sit at the end of its clause. Use that word order to decide, in the longer lines, which word must be the verb and which must be the noun it acts on.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: line up the two texts

Hittite and English tell the same story in the same order, so the first job is to cut both into matching pieces. Working stanza by stanza gives roughly:

HittiteEnglish
našta illuyankan ḫattešnaz šarā kallištaAnd he called up the snake from the hole
kāšawa ezenan iyamiBehold the feast I'm making!
nuwa adanna akuwanna eḫuCome to eat and to drink!
našta illuyankaš qadu dumumeššu šarā úērAnd the snake came up with his sons
nuza eter ekuerAnd they ate and drank
našta palḫan ḫūmandan ekuerAnd they drank all the kettles
ne namma ḫattešnaš kattanta nūmān pānziAnd they could no longer go down into the hole again
ḫupašiyašša úitAnd Hupasiyas came
nu illuyankan išḫimanta kalēliētand tied the snake with a rope
imaš úit nukán illuyankan kuentaThe Stormgod came and killed the snake
dingirmešša kattišši ešerand the gods were with him

Every English sentence starts with "And", and every Hittite line starts with a short word beginning with n-: našta, nuwa, nuza, ne, nu. That is the sentence connector, so našta means "and".

Step 2: the snake and the hole

The word for "snake" appears three times: illuyankan (twice, where the snake is the thing being called up or killed), and illuyankaš (where the snake is the one doing the coming up). So the stem is illuyanka- and the ending tells you the snake's job in the sentence. In grammar terms, the subject is the doer and the direct object is the thing the action happens to. illuyankaš is the subject form, so it translates "snake"; and the two endings we have just isolated are -aš = subject and -an = direct object.

Two other words confirm this. imaš "the Stormgod" takes -aš and is the doer of "came" and "killed". And palḫan ḫūmandan "all the kettles" both take -an, because the kettles are what got drunk.

"Hole" appears as ḫattešnaz "from the hole" and ḫattešnaš "into the hole", so its stem is ḫattešn-. The plain dictionary form offered in the list, ḫatteššar, is therefore the one that means "hole".

Step 3: singular and plural past-tense verbs

Compare the verb "came":

  • úēr in "the snake came up with his sons" — more than one comer
  • úit in "Hupasiyas came" and "The Stormgod came" — one comer

Same stem ú-, different endings, and the only difference in English is how many people are doing it. So -ēr marks a past-tense verb with a plural subject ("they came") and -it marks one with a singular subject ("he came"). That gives úit = "came" for F1, and the F2 answers -er/ēr = 3rd person plural past and -it = 3rd person singular past.

Now "And they ate and drank" is eter ekuer — two verbs, both with the plural ending -er. English gives them in the order "ate", "drank", so eter = "ate" and ekuer = "drank". The next line, našta palḫan ḫūmandan ekuer "And they drank all the kettles", double-checks ekuer = "drank".

Step 4: the leftovers

šarā shows up in exactly the two sentences that contain "up" ("called up the snake", "came up with his sons"), so šarā = "up".

-meš appears in dumumeššu "his sons" and dingirmešša "and the gods" — both plural, so it is the plural marker.

-ša appears on ḫupašiyašša ("And Hupasiyas came") and on dingirmešša ("and the gods were with him"). Both are clause-initial words carrying an extra "and", so -ša is a suffix meaning "and".

Finally, "Come to eat and to drink!" contains adanna akuwanna. An infinitive is the "to" form of a verb, and both Hittite words end in -anna, so that ending marks the infinitive.

Answers

F1: a. (7) ate, b. (2) hole, c. (3) came, d. (1) snake, e. (4) and, f. (5) up, g. (6) drank.

F2: a. (5) subject marker, b. (7) "and", c. (2) plural, d. (3) 3rd plural past, e. (4) direct object, f. (1) infinitive, g. (6) 3rd singular past.

Answer keys taken from the official solution page (F1: a7 b2 c3 d1 e4 f5 g6; F2: a5 b7 c2 d3 e4 f1 g6). Keys are written as the printed option number in parentheses, with the bare digit (and, for F1, the English word) as accepted variants; no 'choices' array was used so that keys stay verbatim with the solution. Point split is unofficial: the booklet gives 15 points with no per-item breakdown, so 14 blanks got 1 point each and F2.7 got 2 to reach 15 — adjust if a breakdown exists.
